# Bālapaṇḍita Sutta (MN 129 (PTS MN iii 163))

**ID:** MN 129 (PTS MN iii 163)  
**Section:** Majjhimanikāya (mn)  
**Collection:** Sutta  
**Title (Pali):** Bālapaṇḍita Sutta  
**Title (English, from literature):** The Foolish and the Astute  
**PTS:** MN iii 163  
**tipitaka.org (CST):** [https://tipitaka.org/romn/cscd/s0203m.mul2.xml](https://tipitaka.org/romn/cscd/s0203m.mul2.xml)

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and catalog data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Bālapaṇḍita Sutta* (MN 129) is a discourse in the *Majjhimanikāya* examining the karmic consequences experienced by the foolish person (*bāla*) and the wise or astute person (*paṇḍita*) [Collins 1998; Marino 2017]. The text expounds how a fool who commits misdeeds of body, speech, and mind experiences three kinds of immediate torment in the present life—social disapproval, a guilty conscience, and terror of judicial punishment and graphic physical torture—before undergoing severe bodily torments in hell or rebirth as an animal [Collins 1998; Radich 2007]. Hell is characterized as an experience that is "utterly unwished for, utterly undesired, utterly disagreeable" [Goodman 2009; Marino 2017]. Conversely, the astute person engages in wholesome conduct, enjoys immediate ease and protection, and is reborn in heaven, an abode described as "utterly wished for, utterly desired, utterly agreeable" [Collins 1998; Goodman 2009]. In illustrating royal majesty and divine bliss, the sutta provides an extensive treatment of the seven treasures (*ratana*) and four blessings of a wheel-turning monarch (*cakkavatti*) [Meisig 2010; Thanissaro 1996].

Scholars note that MN 129 stands alongside the adjacent *Devadūta Sutta* (MN 130) as one of the foundational early cosmographical descriptions of heaven and hell [Marino 2017; Thanissaro 1996]. In modern text-critical analysis, comparative studies suggest that the detailed portrayal of the wheel-turning king's treasures represents an expansion specific to the Pali transmission, as its *Madhyama-āgama* counterpart preserves only a brief enumeration [Meisig 2010]. In another passage describing the fool's regret, parallels in the *Madhyama-āgama*, the Chinese *Nili jing* (T 86), and the Sanskrit *Śrāvakabhūmi* explicitly mention the fool falling sick, indicating that MN 129 likely lost this reference to illness and retained only a description of lying down to rest [Anālayo 2016].

Curated parallels include *Madhyama-āgama* discourse MĀ 199, an independent Chinese translation titled *Nili jing* (T 86, which combines material from MN 129 and MN 130), a Sanskrit Vinaya text (*lo-mvu2*), and the Tibetan *Upāyikā* (Up 2.033) [Marino 2017].

**Parallels and text reuse**

- Full parallels: MA 199 癡慧地
- Passage-level parallels: T 86 泥犁; an2.1; MN 13 (PTS MN i 83) Mahādukkhakkhandha Sutta; AN 3.3 Cintīsutta; AN 3.36 Devadūtasutta; MN 130 (PTS MN iii 178) Devadūta Sutta; Ja 530 Saṅkiccajātaka
- Resembling parallels: Up 2.033; San Lo Mvu 2 Maudgalyāyana’s Visits to Hell
- Mentioned in: Divy 26 Pāṁśupradānāvadānam; Mnd 15 Attadaṇḍasuttaniddesa; Mnd 7 Tissametteyyasuttaniddesa; Cnd 20 Piṅgiyamāṇavapucchāniddesa; Cnd 23 Khaggavisāṇasuttaniddesa; Ne 37 Sāsanapaṭṭhāna; Pe 3 Suttādhiṭṭhānatatiyabhūmi; Pv 10 Khallāṭiyapetivatthu; Kv 20.3 Nirayapālakathā; Pv 19 Dhanapālaseṭṭhipetavatthu; Pv 38 Nandakapetavatthu

**Sources**

- [Collins 1998] Steven Collins, Nirvana and Other Buddhist Felicities: Utopias of the Pali Imaginaire (1998) — Outline of the discourse's teachings on immediate and future consequences of actions for fools and the wise.
- [Goodman 2009] Charles Goodman, Consequences of Compassion: An Interpretation and Defense of Buddhist Ethics (2009) — Passage on the rebirth in heaven and its characterization as utterly desired and agreeable.
- [Radich 2007] Michael David Radich, The Somatics of Liberation: Ideas about Embodiment in Buddhism from Its Origins to the Fifth Century C.E. (2007) — Discussion of the three kinds of suffering of fools in the present life and bodily torments in hell.
- [Marino 2017] Joseph A. Marino, Metaphor and Pedagogy in Early Buddhist Literature: Two Sutras from Senior Collection of Gāndhārī Manuscripts (2017) — Contextualization of MN 129 as an early hell cosmography and details on Chinese parallels like T 86.
- [Anālayo 2016] Bhikkhu Anālayo, Mindfully Facing Disease and Death (2016) — Textual comparison regarding the motif of the fool falling sick prior to death across MĀ, T 86, and Śrāvakabhūmi.
- [Meisig 2010] Konrad Meisig, Translating Buddhist Chinese: Problems and Prospects (2010) — Analysis of textual expansion regarding the seven treasures of the wheel-turning king compared with the Madhyama-āgama.
- [Thanissaro 1996] Thanissaro Bhikkhu, The Wings to Awakening: An Anthology from the Pali Canon (1996) — References to heaven and hell descriptions and the seven treasures of the universal monarch.
